Gao K.lab_name: Department of Urology, Xi'an People's Hospital (Xi'an Fourth Hospital), School of Medicine, Northwest University (Xi'an, Shaanxi, China)
Gao K.role: Urology researcher at Xi'an People's Hospital and first author of a 2026 multicentre study showing that the fat content of TSC kidney tumours predicts how well they shrink on everolimus
Gao K.sub: Department of Urology, Xi'an People's Hospital (Xi'an Fourth Hospital), Northwest University · also listed at the State Key Laboratory of Cancer Biology, Air Force Medical University, Xi'an (2026)
story: Tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC) is a genetic disease in which the brake on mTORC1, the cell's growth-control complex, is missing. One result is angiomyolipoma, a benign kidney tumour made of blood vessels, smooth muscle and fat that can grow large and bleed. Everolimus, a drug that blocks mTORC1, is the standard medical treatment. Ke Gao is first author of a prospective study from several Chinese hospitals that followed 183 patients with these tumours (GAO2026B).

Everolimus cut tumour volume by half or more in 44% of patients after 3 months and in 83% after 6 months. Tumours with little fat shrank better than fat-rich ones, which makes sense if the drug acts mainly on the growing muscle and vessel cells rather than on the fat. A lower dose seemed to work about as well and caused fewer mouth ulcers, but that comparison was exploratory and not randomised, so it needs a proper trial. Tumours grew back when treatment stopped.

On PubMed, Gao's other recent papers come from the same urology department at Xi'an People's Hospital, part of Northwest University's School of Medicine. They include a 2025 rat study on how a high-salt diet raises blood pressure and cholesterol through the immune signal IL-17, and a 2026 review on gut bacteria in cachexia, the wasting syndrome of cancer, written with the State Key Laboratory of Cancer Biology at the Air Force Medical University. No personal institutional page was found, so the position shown is the one on the papers.

highlights.GAO2026B: First author of the multicentre prospective cohort of 183 patients, which linked lower tumour fat content to a better response to everolimus.

Gao K.note: No web profile found; current position taken from 2026 PubMed affiliations.

Ni J.lab_name: Department of Urology, Urology and Nephrology Hospital, Xi'an People's Hospital (Xi'an Fourth Hospital), Northwest University (Xi'an, Shaanxi, China)
Ni J.role: Urologist at Xi'an People's Hospital and senior author of a 2026 multicentre study of everolimus for TSC kidney tumours, with further work on prostate cancer
Ni J.sub: Department of Urology, Urology and Nephrology Hospital, Xi'an People's Hospital (Xi'an Fourth Hospital), Northwest University
story: Jianxin Ni is the last author, usually the person who leads the project, of a 2026 prospective study from several Chinese centres on everolimus for kidney angiomyolipomas in tuberous sclerosis complex (GAO2026B). In TSC the brake on mTORC1, the cell's growth-control complex, is missing, and everolimus puts part of that brake back. In 183 patients the drug shrank tumours by half or more in 44% at 3 months and 83% at 6 months. Tumours with little fat responded better than fat-rich ones, so a scan of tumour fat could help predict who benefits. A lower dose looked similar and caused fewer mouth ulcers, but only in an exploratory, non-randomised comparison. Tumours regrew after the drug was stopped.

PubMed lists about ten papers with Ni at the urology department of Xi'an People's Hospital since 2023. They include a 2026 study in cells and mice showing that the protein PEAK1 helps prostate cancer resist the chemotherapy drug docetaxel by pushing nearby immune cells, macrophages, into a tumour-helping state, and a 2025 rat study on salt, IL-17 and cholesterol. No personal institutional page was found, so the position shown is the one on these papers.

highlights.GAO2026B: Last author who led the multicentre cohort linking tumour fat content to everolimus response in TSC angiomyolipoma.

Ni J.note: No web profile found; current position taken from 2025-2026 PubMed affiliations.

Okazaki H.lab_name: Faculty of Pharmaceutical Sciences, Daiichi University of Pharmacy (Fukuoka, Japan)
Okazaki H.role: Pharmacologist at Daiichi University of Pharmacy in Fukuoka who studies how the body clock sets the daily rhythm of mTOR in tumours and how to time cancer drugs to match it
Okazaki H.sub: Associate Professor, Faculty of Pharmaceutical Sciences, Daiichi University of Pharmacy (2026) · Lecturer (2020–2024) and Assistant Professor (2015–2019) at the same faculty · Graduate School of Pharmaceutical Sciences, Kyushu University, with Shigehiro Ohdo (to 2013)
story: Hiroyuki Okazaki is first author of a 2013 study from Shigehiro Ohdo's chronopharmacology group at Kyushu University (OKA2013). Chronopharmacology asks whether the time of day a drug is given changes what it does. In mice carrying kidney tumours, the amount of mTOR protein and its active, phosphorylated form rose and fell over 24 hours. The circadian clock set this rhythm through Fbxw7, an enzyme that tags mTOR for destruction. When the mTOR blocker everolimus was given at the time of day when mTOR was high, the mice survived longer than with the same dose at other times. The result is in mice; it has not been tested as a dosing schedule in people.

Okazaki's earlier papers with the Ohdo group (from 2010) also deal with daily rhythms in tumours and the brain, for example a clock-driven rhythm in the transferrin receptor that brings iron into colon cancer cells, and clock disruption in a mouse model of Parkinson's disease. From about 2015 Okazaki's papers list the Department of Molecular Biology at Daiichi University of Pharmacy in Fukuoka, still working with Kyushu colleagues on clock-timed drug delivery.

Japan's national research database lists Okazaki as Associate Professor in the Faculty of Pharmaceutical Sciences at Daiichi University in 2026, after posts there as assistant professor and lecturer. Okazaki's grants continue the same theme: using mTOR and the clock to design cancer chronotherapy, timing pain treatment to daily rhythms, and testing Kampo herbal medicines on mTOR in cancer cells.

highlights.OKA2013: First author: showed in tumour-bearing mice that the clock drives a 24-hour mTOR rhythm through Fbxw7 and that dosing everolimus at the mTOR peak improved survival.

Okazaki H.note: KAKEN names the employer 'Daiichi University, College/Faculty of Pharmaceutical Sciences'; PubMed uses 'Daiichi University of Pharmacy'. Lab_name uses the PubMed form.

Nadon NL.lab_name: Division of Aging Biology, National Institute on Aging, National Institutes of Health (Bethesda, Maryland, USA)
Nadon NL.role: Scientist and programme official at the US National Institute on Aging who oversaw research resources for aging biology and helped run the Interventions Testing Program that found rapamycin extends mouse lifespan
Nadon NL.sub: Division of Aging Biology, National Institute on Aging (at the time of the studies) · Chief, Biological Resources Branch (listed 2013) · earlier research at NINDS, NIH, on myelin genetics (1990)
story: Nancy Nadon appears in this Atlas as a co-author on five reports from the Interventions Testing Program (ITP), which the National Institute on Aging (NIA) funds to test possible anti-aging drugs in mice. The ITP runs each test at three sites at once, in genetically mixed mice, so that a result is less likely to be a quirk of one lab or one mouse strain. The most famous result is HAR2009: rapamycin, which blocks the growth-control complex mTORC1, extended lifespan in both sexes even when feeding started late in life. Later reports showed the gain depends on dose and is larger in females (MIL2014), and that resveratrol, simvastatin, green tea extract, curcumin and several other popular compounds did not extend lifespan (MIL2011, STR2012). Acarbose, 17-alpha-estradiol and NDGA did, mostly in males (HAR2014).

Nadon's role was on the funding and organising side. An archived NIA page from 2013 lists Nadon as Chief of the Biological Resources Branch in the Division of Aging Biology, responsible for resource contracts and aged animal resources. Nadon wrote a 2006 review on how to design rodent lifespan studies, describing the problems the ITP had to solve, and was first author of a 2016 overview of the programme with the three site leaders.

Earlier, Nadon did laboratory research. A 1990 paper from NINDS at the NIH, as first author, traced a point mutation in a myelin protein gene that blocks the development of oligodendrocytes, the cells that insulate nerve fibres. The latest PubMed papers date from 2016 to 2018, and no current position could be confirmed.

highlights.HAR2009: Co-author from the NIA, which funds and coordinates the ITP: rapamycin fed from 600 days of age extended mouse lifespan in both sexes.
highlights.MIL2011: Co-author from the NIA: in the same ITP design, rapamycin extended lifespan while resveratrol and simvastatin did not.
highlights.STR2012: Co-author from the NIA on the ITP report in which five popular longevity compounds had no significant effect on lifespan.
highlights.HAR2014: Co-author from the NIA on the ITP report in which acarbose, 17-alpha-estradiol and NDGA extended lifespan, mainly in males.
highlights.MIL2014: Co-author from the NIA on the ITP study showing that rapamycin's lifespan effect depends on dose and sex.

Nadon NL.note: Current position not confirmed; last PubMed papers 2016-2018. May have retired from NIA.

Saucedo LJ.lab_name: Department of Biology, Pacific Lutheran University (Tacoma, Washington, USA)
Saucedo LJ.role: Fruit-fly cell biologist and teacher who, as a postdoc in Bruce Edgar's lab, showed that the small GTPase Rheb drives cell growth in the insulin/TOR pathway
Saucedo LJ.sub: Visiting Assistant Professor of Biology, Pacific Lutheran University · Emeritus Professor of Biology, University of Puget Sound (faculty 2003–2024) · Postdoc and research affiliate, Fred Hutchinson Cancer Research Center (1999–2006) · PhD, University of Wisconsin-Madison (1999)
story: Leslie Saucedo is first author of a 2003 paper from Bruce Edgar's lab at the Fred Hutchinson Cancer Research Center in Seattle (SAU2003). Working in the fruit fly Drosophila, the team found that Rheb, a small switch protein of the GTPase family, makes cells grow bigger when it is overactive and smaller when it is missing. Genetic tests placed Rheb in the insulin/TOR network, the system that tells cells whether there is enough food and growth signal to build more protein. The same year other groups showed that the tumour suppressors TSC1 and TSC2 act by switching Rheb off, so Rheb became the direct link between growth signals and TOR. This was work in flies; the human version of the pathway was confirmed later by others.

Saucedo trained in microbiology at the University of Illinois and earned a PhD in Cellular and Molecular Biology at the University of Wisconsin-Madison in 1999, studying the MDM2 cancer gene and the cell's response to UV damage. Postdoctoral work at the Fred Hutchinson Center from 1999 to 2003, and a research affiliate post there until 2006, focused on finding new genes that control cell growth in flies.

In 2003 Saucedo joined the University of Puget Sound in Tacoma, rising from visiting assistant professor to full professor (2015) and becoming emeritus in 2024. Research there, much of it with undergraduates, used flies to study how the phosphatase PRL-1, the Src and Ras cancer genes, redox balance and autophagy affect growth. Saucedo now teaches as a visiting assistant professor in biology at Pacific Lutheran University.

highlights.SAU2003: First author: showed in Drosophila that Rheb promotes cell growth as part of the insulin/TOR signalling network.

Saucedo LJ.note: Tacoma, Washington, USA is a new location string (not in canonical list).

de Mol J.lab_name: Aging and Immunity group (Foks lab), Division of BioTherapeutics, Leiden Academic Centre for Drug Research, Leiden University (Leiden, Netherlands)
de Mol J.role: Immunologist at Leiden University who studies how the aging immune system, especially aged B cells, drives atherosclerosis, and first author of a 2026 study of rapamycin as an immune rejuvenator in old mice
de Mol J.sub: Postdoc, Aging and Immunity group, Division of BioTherapeutics, LACDR, Leiden University · PhD candidate in Amanda Foks's group, Leiden University
story: Atherosclerosis is the build-up of fatty, inflamed plaques in artery walls, and it gets worse with age partly because the immune system ages too. Jill de Mol is first author of a 2026 study from Amanda Foks's group in Leiden that gave rapamycin, which blocks the growth-control complex mTORC1, to old mice prone to atherosclerosis (JIN2026C). The plaques held fewer macrophages and T cells. Killer CD8 T cells shifted from an aggressive effector state to a calmer memory state, regulatory T cells that dampen inflammation increased in the aorta, and the antibody-making arm of immunity quietened, with fewer germinal-centre B cells, plasma cells and autoantibodies. Age-associated B cells dropped and the immune cells in the aorta looked less senescent, or worn out. The authors read this as rapamycin acting like an immune rejuvenation therapy. It is a mouse result; whether the same happens in older people is untested.

de Mol did a PhD in Foks's Aging and Immunity group at the Leiden Academic Centre for Drug Research and continues there as a postdoc. The group's work centres on aged B cell immunity in the plaque environment: the team found age-associated B cells in the blood and plaques of people with coronary artery disease and wants to understand them well enough to design targeted immune therapies for heart disease. In 2024 de Mol won a best poster award at the GEMSEQ meeting.

highlights.JIN2026C: First author: showed in aged atherosclerotic mice that rapamycin reduced plaque inflammation and reset T and B cell responses toward a younger profile.

de Mol J.note: Atlas sid JIN2026C has de Mol J as first author; the sid prefix does not match the name, curator may want to check.

Panchaud N.lab_name: De Virgilio lab, Department of Biology, Division of Biochemistry, University of Fribourg (Fribourg, Canton of Fribourg, Switzerland)
Panchaud N.role: Biochemist who, during a PhD with Claudio De Virgilio in Fribourg, showed that the yeast SEACIT complex switches off TORC1 when amino acids run out, and who later moved into clinical drug development at Novartis
Panchaud N.sub: PhD in Biochemistry, University of Fribourg (De Virgilio lab, at the time of the study) · Associate Clinical Scientist, Novartis (listed 2018; joined 2015 through its postgraduate programme)
story: Cells must stop growing when food runs short. In 2013, Nicolas Panchaud, working in Claudio De Virgilio's yeast lab at the University of Fribourg, was first author of a paper that found one of the switches (PAN2013). TORC1, the yeast version of the growth-control complex mTORC1, is turned on by small proteins called Rag GTPases (Gtr1 and Gtr2 in yeast) when amino acids are plentiful. The team showed that a protein group they named SEACIT acts as a GAP, an 'off button' that makes Gtr1 switch itself off, and that cells without it cannot shut down TORC1 when amino acids are removed. The human counterpart, GATOR1, was described in the same year, so the yeast work helped establish that this brake is shared from yeast to humans. The experiments were done in yeast cells.

Panchaud earned a PhD in Biochemistry at the University of Fribourg. According to a 2018 University of Zurich career event page, Panchaud then joined Novartis in 2015 through its two-year postgraduate programme and was working as an associate clinical scientist, a role in planning and running clinical trials. No more recent position could be confirmed.

highlights.PAN2013: First author: showed in yeast that the SEACIT complex is a GAP for the Rag GTPase Gtr1 and is needed to switch off TORC1 when amino acids are scarce.

Panchaud N.note: Novartis role confirmed only from a 2018 event page; current position unknown, so lab_name keeps the Fribourg affiliation of the study.

Saxena A.lab_name: Institute of Medical Genetics, Division of Cancer and Genetics, School of Medicine, Cardiff University (Cardiff, Wales, United Kingdom)
Saxena A.role: Clinical research fellow at Cardiff University who coordinated TRON, a placebo-controlled trial testing whether everolimus improves memory and thinking in adults with tuberous sclerosis complex
Saxena A.sub: Clinical Research Fellow, Institute of Medical Genetics, Cardiff University · PhD, Cardiff University (2021), with Julian Sampson
story: Everolimus, an mTOR blocker, is approved for the tumours and seizures of tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC). Many people with TSC also have problems with memory, attention and planning, and mouse studies suggested mTOR blockers might help. Anurag Saxena is first author of the main report of TRON, a trial run from Cardiff that tested this in adults with TSC (SAX2026). Thirty-eight patients were randomised, two on everolimus for every one on placebo, for 24 weeks. Most people in both groups improved on the thinking tests (87% on everolimus, 75% on placebo), which points to practice and placebo effects rather than a clear drug benefit. Side effects were more common on everolimus. The trial was small, so a modest effect cannot be ruled out, but it gives no support for prescribing everolimus for cognition alone.

Saxena coordinated TRON and carried out the clinical assessments as part of a PhD at Cardiff University, completed in 2021 with a thesis on the effect of everolimus on neurocognitive aspects of TSC. The thesis thanks Julian Sampson, the senior author of the trial report, and Derek Jones. Saxena works as a Clinical Research Fellow at Cardiff's Institute of Medical Genetics, with papers on TSC epilepsy, everolimus side effects and the clinical features of mTOR pathway gene mutations.

highlights.SAX2026: First author: reported the TRON randomised trial, in which everolimus did not clearly beat placebo for memory and thinking in adults with TSC.

Sinclair LV.lab_name: Division of Cell Signalling and Immunology, School of Life Sciences, University of Dundee (Dundee, Scotland, United Kingdom)
Sinclair LV.role: T cell immunologist at the University of Dundee who works out how amino acid supply, through transporters such as SLC7A5, feeds mTORC1 and decides what activated T cells become
Sinclair LV.sub: Senior Researcher, Cell Signalling and Immunology, University of Dundee · long-time member of Doreen Cantrell's group · PhD, University of Dundee · BSc in Immunology, University of Edinburgh
story: When a T cell meets its target, it must grow fast, divide many times and switch on its killing machinery. All of that needs amino acids. Linda Sinclair is first author of a 2013 paper from Doreen Cantrell's group in Dundee that showed how the T cell gets them (SIN2013). Signals from the antigen receptor, the T cell's sensor for infection, switch on the transporter SLC7A5, a channel that carries large amino acids such as leucine into the cell. Mouse T cells lacking SLC7A5 could not keep mTORC1, the growth-control complex, active or keep making the growth protein c-Myc, and they failed to turn into effector cells. The study, done in mouse T cells, made amino acid transport a control point for immune responses rather than a passive supply line.

Sinclair grew up partly in Sweden, studied immunology at the University of Edinburgh and did a PhD at the University of Dundee. Since then Sinclair has worked with Doreen Cantrell on how nutrients steer T lymphocytes. An earlier paper (Nature Immunology, 2008) showed that mTOR controls where T cells travel in the body, and later work found that SLC7A5-driven methionine uptake acts as a metabolic checkpoint for effector T cells (eLife, 2019).

The University of Dundee lists Sinclair as a Senior Researcher in the Division of Cell Signalling and Immunology. Current topics include mTOR signalling, amino acid uptake and autophagy in CD8 killer T cells, with related work on MAIT cells, B cell metabolism and iron handling in dendritic cells.

highlights.SIN2013: First author: showed in mouse T cells that antigen receptors switch on the SLC7A5 amino acid transporter, which sustains mTORC1 and c-Myc and is needed for effector differentiation.

de Vries PJ.lab_name: Division of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry and Centre for Autism Research in Africa, University of Cape Town (Cape Town, South Africa)
de Vries PJ.role: Child and adolescent psychiatrist at the University of Cape Town known for work on TAND, the behavioural, learning and mental-health problems of tuberous sclerosis complex, and co-author of major everolimus trials in TSC
de Vries PJ.sub: Sue Struengmann Professor of Child & Adolescent Psychiatry, University of Cape Town · Founding Director, Centre for Autism Research in Africa · President, International Society for Autism Research · earlier clinical and research career in the United Kingdom (PhD, University of Cambridge)
story: Petrus de Vries appears in this Atlas on two trials of everolimus, an mTOR blocker, in tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC), the genetic disease in which mTORC1 runs unchecked. EXIST-3 (FRE2016) was a large phase 3 trial in 366 children and adults whose focal seizures had not responded to standard drugs. Adding everolimus at a higher blood level halved seizure frequency in 40% of patients, against 15% on placebo, and it became the basis for approving the drug for TSC epilepsy. TRON (SAX2026) asked a harder question in adults: does everolimus improve memory and thinking? Both everolimus and placebo groups improved, so the trial found no clear drug effect on cognition.

de Vries studied medicine at Stellenbosch University in South Africa, then trained in psychiatry and in child and adolescent psychiatry in the United Kingdom and earned a PhD in developmental neuroscience at the University of Cambridge. Work on TSC began in 1997, with a focus on its behavioural, intellectual, psychiatric and learning problems, now grouped under the name TSC-Associated Neuropsychiatric Disorders (TAND), on which de Vries has led international consensus recommendations.

In 2012 de Vries returned to South Africa as the Sue Struengmann Professor of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry at the University of Cape Town and became founding director of the Centre for Autism Research in Africa. Current work covers autism and child mental health in low- and middle-income settings, alongside the TSC programme. In 2014 de Vries received the Manuel R Gomez Award from the TSC community.

highlights.FRE2016: Co-author of EXIST-3, the phase 3 trial showing that adjunctive everolimus reduces treatment-resistant seizures in TSC.
highlights.SAX2026: Co-author of the TRON trial report, which found no clear benefit of everolimus over placebo for neuropsychological deficits in TSC.

de Vries PJ.note: INSAR presidency is from the ICNA speaker page (date not given).

McNeill M.lab_name: Division of Hematology-Oncology, Department of Pediatrics, The Hospital for Sick Children (Toronto, Ontario, Canada)
McNeill M.role: Paediatric haematology researcher at SickKids in Toronto and first author of a 2026 cohort study of sirolimus for Evans syndrome and other autoimmune blood-count disorders in children
McNeill M.sub: Division of Hematology-Oncology, Department of Pediatrics, The Hospital for Sick Children, and Department of Pediatrics, University of Toronto (at the time of the study)
story: In Evans syndrome the immune system attacks the body's own blood cells, usually red cells and platelets together, so children can become anaemic and bruise or bleed easily. Steroids often help only for a while. Sirolimus (rapamycin) blocks mTOR in overactive immune cells and has been tried as a gentler long-term option. Maggie McNeill is first author of a 2026 retrospective study from the Hospital for Sick Children (SickKids) in Toronto that looked back at children treated with sirolimus for Evans syndrome and for autoimmune cytopenias, low blood counts, linked to other conditions (MCNEILL2026). The authors report that sirolimus was effective. A look-back study from one centre cannot show how much of the improvement was due to the drug, and the abstract was not yet indexed when this profile was written, so the exact numbers are still to be added.

PubMed lists McNeill in the Division of Hematology-Oncology at SickKids and the Department of Pediatrics at the University of Toronto, working with senior author Manuel Carcao. No other papers clearly by the same person were found, and no personal institutional page was found, so the position shown is the one on the paper.

highlights.MCNEILL2026: First author of the single-centre retrospective cohort reporting that sirolimus is effective for paediatric Evans syndrome and secondary autoimmune cytopenias.

McNeill M.note: Only one PubMed paper firmly tied to this person; a 2020 gynaecologic oncology paper by a Maggie McNeill at McMaster was not attributed (different field).

Ouyang G.lab_name: Division of Hepatobiliary Surgery, The First Affiliated Hospital of Guangxi Medical University (Nanning, China)
Ouyang G.role: Liver surgery researcher at Guangxi Medical University and senior author of a 2026 study in which the plant compound notoginsenoside R1 eased paracetamol liver injury by boosting autophagy
Ouyang G.sub: Division of Hepatobiliary Surgery, The First Affiliated Hospital of Guangxi Medical University (2026) · Department of General Surgery, Liuzhou People's Hospital affiliated to Guangxi Medical University (2024)
story: An overdose of acetaminophen (paracetamol) is one of the commonest causes of sudden liver failure. Guoqing Ouyang is last author of a 2026 study testing notoginsenoside R1, a compound from the medicinal plant Panax notoginseng, in this kind of injury (LIS2026). The compound reduced liver cell death and oxidative damage, and it worked by boosting autophagy, the cell's recycling system, through changes in MAPK and mTOR signalling. mTOR normally holds autophagy back, so easing it lets damaged cells clean up. The work was done in laboratory models; there is no evidence yet that the compound helps people with overdose.

Ouyang's PubMed record is in liver disease at Guangxi Medical University in Nanning. Recent papers include a 2024 study, as first author from Liuzhou People's Hospital affiliated to the university, that grouped liver cancers by genes of a cell-death programme called PANoptosis and built a survival score, and work with Songqing He's hepatobiliary surgery group on alcohol-related liver disease. A Frontiers profile lists Ouyang at the Division of Hepatobiliary Surgery of the First Affiliated Hospital as a doctoral-level researcher, but no institutional page was found, so the position shown is the one on the 2026 paper.

highlights.LIS2026: Last author: led the study showing that notoginsenoside R1 eases acetaminophen liver injury by promoting protective autophagy via MAPK/mTOR.

Ouyang G.note: Nanning, China used from canonical list (PubMed says Nanning, Guangxi).

Banerjee C.lab_name: Division of Neuroscience, Department of Pharmacology, ISF College of Pharmacy (Moga, Punjab, India)
Banerjee C.role: Pharmacology researcher at ISF College of Pharmacy in Punjab who writes reviews on signalling pathways and repurposed drugs for multiple sclerosis and other brain diseases
Banerjee C.sub: Division of Neuroscience, Department of Pharmacology, ISF College of Pharmacy, affiliated to IK Gujral Punjab Technical University (2026, at the time of the study)
story: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a disease in which the immune system attacks myelin, the fatty insulation around nerve fibres in the brain and spinal cord. Chandrayee Banerjee is first author of a 2026 review on how two signalling systems talk to each other in MS (BANERJEE2026). One is the PI3K/Akt/mTOR pathway, which controls growth and metabolism in immune cells and in the oligodendrocytes that make myelin. The other is JAK/STAT, which carries signals from inflammatory messengers into the cell nucleus. The review argues that the two pathways reinforce each other in driving Th17 inflammatory T cells and microglia, the brain's immune cells, and that mTOR has two faces in MS: it helps oligodendrocytes mature and rebuild myelin, but too much of it feeds damage. It is a review of earlier studies, not new experiments, and drugs that hit both pathways at once have not been tested in people with MS.

PubMed lists three 2026 papers with Banerjee, all from Sidharth Mehan's neuroscience group in the Department of Pharmacology at ISF College of Pharmacy in Moga. The other two are reviews on repurposing older drugs for brain disease: the antihistamine clemastine as a promoter of myelin repair, and the osteoporosis drug raloxifene as a possible neuroprotective agent. No institutional profile page was found, so the position shown is the one on these papers.

highlights.BANERJEE2026: First author of the review mapping crosstalk between PI3K/Akt/mTOR and JAK/STAT signalling in multiple sclerosis.

Banerjee C.note: Likely a postgraduate researcher; career stage not confirmed by any official page.

Young LR.lab_name: Division of Pulmonary and Sleep Medicine, Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, and Perelman School of Medicine, University of Pennsylvania (Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, USA)
Young LR.role: Lung physician-scientist who helped run the first sirolimus trials in lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM) and now leads pulmonary medicine at the Children's Hospital of Philadelphia
Young LR.sub: Chief, Division of Pulmonary and Sleep Medicine, Children's Hospital of Philadelphia · Professor of Pediatrics, Perelman School of Medicine, University of Pennsylvania · Vanderbilt University (from 2011) · University of Cincinnati and Cincinnati Children's Hospital (fellowship and six years on faculty)
story: Lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM) is a rare lung disease, almost only in women, in which abnormal muscle-like cells with an overactive mTOR pathway slowly fill the lungs with cysts. It can also occur in tuberous sclerosis complex, together with kidney tumours called angiomyolipomas. Lisa Young was a co-author of the two Cincinnati-led trials that first tested sirolimus (rapamycin) against these problems. In the 2008 trial (BIS2008), a year of sirolimus shrank kidney angiomyolipomas in patients with TSC or LAM, though they grew back after the drug stopped. The larger MILES trial (MCC2011) compared sirolimus with placebo in 89 women with LAM: lung function held steady on sirolimus while it kept falling on placebo, and the benefit faded once the drug was stopped. MILES led to sirolimus becoming the standard treatment for LAM.

Young studied at the University of Virginia, earned an MD at Duke University and trained there in both paediatrics and internal medicine. A double fellowship in paediatric pulmonology and adult pulmonary and critical care followed at Cincinnati Children's Hospital and the University of Cincinnati, where Young then spent six years on the faculty, the period of the two trials. In 2011 Young moved to Vanderbilt University and later to Philadelphia.

Young is now Chief of the Division of Pulmonary and Sleep Medicine at the Children's Hospital of Philadelphia and Professor of Pediatrics at the University of Pennsylvania. Research topics include LAM and other rare lung diseases such as Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome and neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia of infancy, as well as lung development, injury and repair.

highlights.BIS2008: Co-author of the Cincinnati trial showing that sirolimus shrinks kidney angiomyolipomas in TSC and LAM.
highlights.MCC2011: Co-author of the MILES trial, in which sirolimus stabilised lung function in women with LAM while it was taken.

Saci A.lab_name: Division of Signal Transduction, Department of Medicine, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center and Harvard Medical School (Boston, Massachusetts, USA)
Saci A.role: Cell biologist who, in Christopher Carpenter's lab at Beth Israel Deaconess, found that the small GTPase Rac1 binds mTOR and helps set the activity and location of both mTOR complexes
Saci A.sub: Division of Signal Transduction, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center and Harvard Medical School, Carpenter lab (2003–2011, at the time of the study)
story: mTOR works inside two different protein complexes. mTORC1 controls cell growth and protein making, and mTORC2 controls cell shape and survival signals. Abdelhafid Saci is first author of a 2011 paper from Christopher Carpenter's lab at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center in Boston (SAC2011). The team found that Rac1, a small switch protein best known for reorganising the cell's internal skeleton, binds mTOR directly and is needed for both complexes to work properly. Rac1 helped bring the complexes to the right places inside the cell, at membranes, and cells without Rac1 activity grew smaller. The work was done in cultured cells. It linked the machinery of cell shape and movement to the machinery of cell growth.

Saci's earlier PubMed record with the Carpenter lab includes a 2003 paper in Immunity showing that the kinase BTK brings lipid-making enzymes to the cell membrane in B cells, which links Saci's work to the PI3K signalling system that sits upstream of mTOR. No current institutional page could be confirmed, so the affiliation shown is the one on the Atlas paper.

highlights.SAC2011: First author: showed in cultured cells that Rac1 binds mTOR, regulates both mTORC1 and mTORC2, guides their location and controls cell size.

Saci A.note: PubMed also lists 'Abdel Saci' at Bristol Myers Squibb translational medicine (2018-2021) and an 'A. Saci' at INSERM U428 Paris (1999, PI3K in platelets); these may be the same person but no source linked them, so they were left out.

Mugale MN.lab_name: Division of Toxicology and Experimental Medicine, CSIR-Central Drug Research Institute (Lucknow, India)
Mugale MN.role: Toxicologist at CSIR-CDRI in Lucknow whose group studies how organs such as the liver and lung are injured and scarred, and how hormones and drugs change that process
Mugale MN.sub: Division of Toxicology and Experimental Medicine, CSIR-Central Drug Research Institute, Lucknow · also affiliated with the Academy of Scientific and Innovative Research (AcSIR)
story: Fibrosis is scarring: after repeated injury, an organ fills with stiff connective tissue and stops working well. Madhav Mugale is last author, the group leader, of a 2026 rat study on liver fibrosis caused by the toxin carbon tetrachloride (VER2026). Male rats given testosterone kept their mitochondria, the cell's power plants, in better shape, and their autophagy, the cell's recycling system, kept flowing: the protein p62 did not pile up and markers of working autophagy such as LC3B and Beclin-1 stayed higher. mTOR activity was maintained. Castrated rats did worse, with more damaged mitochondria and more cell death. The study suggests that male hormones help the liver cope with toxic injury in rats; it did not test people.

PubMed lists more than 90 papers with Mugale, all from the Division of Toxicology and Experimental Medicine at CSIR-CDRI, a national drug research institute in Lucknow, from 2019 onward. They cover safety testing of drug ingredients, models of lung and liver fibrosis, and collaborations with CDRI pharmacology groups on diabetes and insulin resistance in mice. Mugale is also affiliated with the Academy of Scientific and Innovative Research (AcSIR), which runs CSIR's doctoral programmes. No official profile page was found, so job title and training are not given.

highlights.VER2026: Last author: led the rat study showing that testosterone preserves mitochondrial health and autophagic flux, with sustained mTOR activity, in toxin-induced liver fibrosis.

Mugale MN.note: PubMed spells the middle name both 'Nilakanth' (older papers) and 'Nilakhanth' (2026); Atlas spelling kept. Job title and training not found.

Meikle L.lab_name: Division of Translational Medicine, Department of Medicine, Brigham and Women's Hospital and Harvard Medical School (Boston, Massachusetts, USA)
Meikle L.role: Researcher in David Kwiatkowski's tuberous sclerosis lab at Brigham and Women's Hospital who built a mouse model of TSC in the brain and showed that mTOR blockers rescue it
Meikle L.sub: Division of Translational Medicine, Brigham and Women's Hospital and Harvard Medical School, Kwiatkowski lab (papers 2005–2009, at the time of the study)
story: In tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC), loss of the TSC1 or TSC2 gene removes the brake on mTORC1, the growth-control complex, and the brain is often hit hardest, with seizures, learning problems and autism. Lynsey Meikle, working in David Kwiatkowski's lab in Boston, first built a mouse in which most nerve cells of the cerebral cortex lose Tsc1 during development. Published in 2007, these mice had enlarged, misplaced neurons, delayed myelination, seizures and a median survival of only 35 days, which made them a model of the human brain disease.

In the Atlas paper (MEI2008), Meikle and colleagues treated these mice with rapamycin and the related drug RAD001 (everolimus). The drugs switched off the overactive mTORC1 signal, restored Akt signalling, and greatly improved survival and brain function. This mouse work was part of the evidence that led to testing mTOR blockers in people with TSC, where everolimus is now used for brain and kidney tumours and for seizures.

Meikle also contributed to a 2009 study with Mustafa Sahin's group showing that neurons lacking the TSC complex suffer high stress in the endoplasmic reticulum, a protein-folding compartment, which rapamycin reversed. No later papers or current position could be found, so the affiliation shown is the one on the Atlas paper.

highlights.MEI2008: First author: showed that rapamycin and RAD001 improve survival and function in a neuronal Tsc1 mouse model of tuberous sclerosis.

Meikle L.note: Web search budget was exhausted before this person was searched; profile is PubMed-only. Current position unknown.

Kraus WE.lab_name: Duke Molecular Physiology Institute and Division of Cardiology, Duke University School of Medicine (Durham, North Carolina, USA)
Kraus WE.role: Cardiologist and exercise scientist at Duke University who leads long-running trials on how exercise and calorie restriction change human health, and senior author of the CALERIE two-year safety report
Kraus WE.sub: Duke Molecular Physiology Institute · Division of Cardiology, Department of Medicine, Duke University School of Medicine · Duke Clinical Research Institute (at the time of the study)
story: Calorie restriction, eating less without malnutrition, slows aging in many animals and lowers mTOR activity. CALERIE (Comprehensive Assessment of Long-term Effects of Reducing Intake of Energy) was the first long trial to test it in healthy, non-obese people. William Kraus is last author of the 2016 report on its safety (ROM2016). Over two years, participants aimed to eat 25% fewer calories. The diet was safe overall, with no rise in serious problems, but bone density fell more than in the control group, so bone health needs watching in anyone who tries long-term restriction.

Kraus's PubMed record runs to hundreds of papers from Duke on exercise, heart and metabolic health. In 2026 Kraus is listed at the Duke Molecular Physiology Institute and the Division of Cardiology, for example on a follow-up of STRRIDE, a supervised exercise trial in older adults, which found that step counts from wearable devices tracked fitness and heart-health measures better than people's own reports of how much they exercised.

highlights.ROM2016: Last author of the CALERIE report showing that two years of 25% calorie restriction was safe in healthy non-obese adults, apart from greater bone density loss.

Nazio F.lab_name: Department of Biology, University of Rome Tor Vergata (Rome, Italy)
Nazio F.role: Cell biologist at the University of Rome Tor Vergata who, in Francesco Cecconi's lab, showed how mTOR keeps autophagy switched off by acting on AMBRA1 and the starter kinase ULK1
Nazio F.sub: Department of Biology, University of Rome Tor Vergata (papers to 2026) · Dulbecco Telethon Institute, Cecconi lab (2013)
story: Autophagy is the cell's recycling system: when food is short, cells wrap up worn-out parts and break them down for raw materials. mTORC1, the growth-control complex, keeps autophagy off when nutrients are plentiful. Francesca Nazio is first author of a 2013 paper from Francesco Cecconi's group at the Dulbecco Telethon Institute in Rome that explained one way it does this (NAZ2013). The kinase ULK1 starts autophagy. To work well it needs the helper protein AMBRA1 and the enzyme TRAF6, which together add ubiquitin chains to ULK1, stabilise it and help it cluster. mTOR phosphorylates AMBRA1 and so blocks this step; when mTOR is switched off, AMBRA1 is freed and autophagy can begin. The experiments were done in cultured cells.

Nazio has stayed at the University of Rome Tor Vergata, with more than 60 papers on PubMed. Recent work includes a 2024 review with Silvia Campello's group on how cancer cells take up mitochondria from healthy neighbours to gain energy and resist treatment, and a 2026 study on how the heme-making enzyme ferrochelatase shapes the metabolism and staying power of CAR T cells used against the childhood cancer neuroblastoma. The current job title could not be confirmed.

highlights.NAZ2013: First author: showed that mTOR blocks autophagy by phosphorylating AMBRA1, preventing TRAF6-driven ubiquitylation, stabilisation and self-association of ULK1.

Nazio F.note: Web search budget was exhausted before this person was searched; profile is PubMed-only. Current position title unknown (Tor Vergata affiliation confirmed to 2026).

Perez K.role: Aging researcher at the Swiss company EPITERNA, linked to Alejandro Ocampo's lab at the University of Lausanne, who builds screening platforms to find drugs that extend lifespan across several species
Perez K.sub: EPITERNA SA, Epalinges · Department of Biomedical Sciences, University of Lausanne, Ocampo lab (papers 2023–2026)
story: Many drugs extend lifespan in one lab animal and then fail in the next. Kevin Perez is first author of a 2026 paper describing a platform built to tackle that problem (PEREZ2026). It tests compounds in yeast, nematode worms, fruit flies, killifish and mice, uses automated imaging and a deep-learning program to spot when each animal dies, and has screened more than 400 compounds under thousands of conditions. By comparing species, it picks out compounds that work in several of them and shows that hits tend to act on known conserved longevity pathways, mTOR among them. The paper is about methods and infrastructure; individual hits still need checking in mammals and eventually people.

PubMed lists Perez with both EPITERNA SA and Alejandro Ocampo's group in the Department of Biomedical Sciences at the University of Lausanne. Earlier work includes a 2023 first-author study showing that mouse models of premature aging with defects in DNA repair have an older 'epigenetic age', measured from DNA methylation, than their real age, unlike other premature aging models, and a 2025 study in which a two-chemical reprogramming cocktail reduced signs of aging in human cells and extended lifespan in worms.

highlights.PEREZ2026: First author of the cross-species screening platform spanning yeast, worms, flies, killifish and mice used to find lifespan-extending compounds that generalise.

Araki K.lab_name: Department of Microbiology and Immunology and Emory Vaccine Center, Emory University (Atlanta, Georgia, USA)
Araki K.role: Immunologist in Rafi Ahmed's group at Emory who discovered that rapamycin improves memory killer T cells, a finding that linked mTOR to vaccine design
Araki K.sub: Department of Microbiology and Immunology, Emory University (papers to 2026) · Emory Vaccine Center, Rafi Ahmed lab (2009)
story: After an infection, most killer CD8 T cells die off, but a few become long-lived memory cells that guard against the same germ in future. Koichi Araki is first author of a 2009 paper from Rafi Ahmed's lab at the Emory Vaccine Center that found mTOR helps decide this fate (ARA2009). In mice infected with a virus, low doses of rapamycin, an mTOR blocker best known as a drug that suppresses the immune system, actually increased the number and quality of memory CD8 T cells. Blocking mTOR inside the T cells themselves had the same effect, and rapamycin also improved T cell memory after vaccination in monkeys. The result changed how immunologists think about mTOR: besides acting as a growth switch, it is a decision point between short-lived effector cells and long-lived memory cells.

Araki has continued at Emory's Department of Microbiology and Immunology. A 2026 study, with Araki as a co-author, tested the idea in an HIV-like vaccine model: rhesus macaques given rapamycin during booster shots of an SIV vaccine had more and better memory CD8 T cells, lower virus levels in the gut and blood after infection, and longer survival. The current job title could not be confirmed.

highlights.ARA2009: First author: showed that mTOR regulates memory CD8 T-cell differentiation and that rapamycin enhances memory responses after infection and vaccination.

Dibbens LM.lab_name: Epilepsy Research Group, Australian Centre for Precision Health, University of South Australia (Adelaide, South Australia, Australia)
Dibbens LM.role: Epilepsy geneticist at the University of South Australia who found that mutations in DEPDC5, part of the GATOR1 brake on mTORC1, cause familial focal epilepsy
Dibbens LM.sub: Epilepsy Research Group, Clinical and Health Sciences, Australian Centre for Precision Health, University of South Australia (papers to 2025)
story: Some families pass down epilepsy in which seizures start in one part of the brain, a different part in different relatives. Leanne Dibbens is first author of a 2013 study that found a gene behind it (DIB2013B). By reading the protein-coding DNA of affected families and tracking which stretch of DNA travelled with the disease, the team found loss-of-function mutations in DEPDC5 in most large families studied and in about 12% of smaller ones. DEPDC5 is part of GATOR1, a complex that switches off mTORC1 when amino acids are scarce, so the finding tied a common form of inherited epilepsy to the mTOR pathway. The study is genetic; it did not measure mTOR activity itself, and the link to mTORC1 rests on the known role of GATOR1.

Dibbens leads epilepsy genetics work in Adelaide, with about 80 papers on PubMed. A 2025 study with the group used the structure of the KCNT1 potassium channel to screen known drugs for ones that block the overactive channel found in severe childhood epilepsies, tested them in cells and in fruit flies carrying the human mutation, and identified antrafenine as a candidate that also reaches the brain in mice.

highlights.DIB2013B: First author: identified loss-of-function DEPDC5 mutations, a GATOR1 subunit, as a cause of familial focal epilepsy with variable foci.

Dibbens LM.note: Web search budget was exhausted before this person was searched; title and training not confirmed.

Karuppasamy M.lab_name: European Molecular Biology Laboratory, Grenoble Outstation (Grenoble, France)
Karuppasamy M.role: Structural biologist who used cryo-electron microscopy at EMBL Grenoble to solve the first structure of yeast TORC2, explaining why it resists rapamycin
Karuppasamy M.sub: European Molecular Biology Laboratory, Grenoble, Schaffitzel group (papers 2016–2020, at the time of the study)
story: TOR works in two complexes. TORC1 is blocked by rapamycin, but TORC2 is not, and for years nobody could see why. Manikandan Karuppasamy is first author of a 2017 study from Christiane Schaffitzel's group at EMBL Grenoble that solved the structure of yeast TORC2 by cryo-electron microscopy, a method that images frozen protein molecules in an electron microscope and combines many pictures into a 3D model (KAR2017). The structure showed the overall layout of the complex and that the protein Avo3 sits over the spot where rapamycin, with its partner FKBP12, would need to bind, which explains the drug's lack of effect. The work was done on purified yeast proteins.

At EMBL Grenoble Karuppasamy also helped solve the cryo-EM structure of a human 48S translation pre-initiation complex, the ribosome machinery that starts protein production (2018), and contributed to a 2020 method for imaging long non-coding RNAs by atomic force microscopy. No later position could be confirmed, so the affiliation shown is the one on the Atlas paper.

highlights.KAR2017: First author: solved the cryo-EM structure of yeast TORC2, revealing its architecture and the structural basis for rapamycin insensitivity.

Kristiansen JB.lab_name: Exercise Biology, Department of Public Health, Aarhus University (Aarhus, Denmark)
Kristiansen JB.role: Exercise biologist at Aarhus University, working with Kristian Vissing, who studies how aging changes muscle's response to mechanical load and to food
Kristiansen JB.sub: Exercise Biology, Department of Public Health, Aarhus University, Vissing group (papers 2025–2026)
story: Muscles grow when they are stretched and loaded, and mTORC1, the growth-control complex, is one of the main switches that turns that signal into new protein. Older muscle often responds less, a problem called anabolic resistance. Jonas Boritz Kristiansen is first author of a 2026 study from Kristian Vissing's exercise biology group at Aarhus University that tested which part of the signal is lost (KRISTIANSEN2026). Muscles from adult and old female mice were stretched in a dish. mTORC1 signalling switched on just as strongly in old muscle as in young, but a second stress pathway, JNK-SMAD2L, responded less with age. So, at least in this mouse model, the mTORC1 sensor for stretch seems to stay intact with age.

Kristiansen's other papers fit the same theme. A 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis, as first author, pooled 46 human studies and found that older adults make muscle protein slightly more slowly than young adults at rest and after a meal, but respond about as well to exercise. A 2025 rat study, with the same group, looked at how weeks of voluntary wheel running affect oxidative stress and DNA repair in the brain. No institutional profile was found, so career stage is not given.

highlights.KRISTIANSEN2026: First author: showed in ex vivo mouse muscle that stretch activates mTORC1 equally in adult and old females while JNK-SMAD2L signalling is blunted with age.
